claims.text: The coating is a dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy.
The as-deposited coating contains interpenetrating nanostructured FCC and BCC regions.
The coating's creep resistance arises primarily from a high density of nanoscale FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
Nanoscale FCC/BCC phase boundaries pin dislocations.
Pinning of dislocations by phase boundaries delays plastic deformation under sustained load.
Processing changes such as annealing can vary phase-boundary density and distribution without changing the overall alloy composition.
Abundant, finely dispersed phase boundaries impede dislocation motion under sustained stress.
Phase-boundary pinning slows both dislocation glide and dislocation climb.
Slower dislocation glide and climb reduce creep deformation relative to a microstructure with fewer or coarser phase boundaries.
A coating with an optimized high phase-boundary density will exhibit significantly less creep strain over a fixed time than a lower-boundary-density coating.
A different thermal treatment can produce a coarser or less abundant population of phase interfaces for use as a baseline.
The proposed phase-boundary-controlled mechanism applies under sustained stress at temperatures up to approximately 0.5Tm when dislocation-based creep dominates.
At extreme temperatures, mechanisms such as grain-boundary sliding may supersede the proposed dislocation-based mechanism.
Grain size and compositional gradients may influence the relationship between phase-boundary density and creep rate.
A lack of statistically significant creep-strain reduction in the high-boundary-density group would falsify the hypothesis.
Observation that phase boundaries do not impede dislocation motion would falsify the proposed mechanism.
